newsitem.title: ANGOLA: New Angolan unity government gets down to work.
newsitem.headline: New Angolan unity government gets down to work.

text.p: Angola's former bitter enemies have got down to work in a power-sharing government after two decades of civil war.
But political and economic change in the battle-scarred country is expected to be slow as the new partners work to overcome years of distrust.
The ruling MPLA and former rebel UNITA last Friday formed a government of national unity as they agreed in a U.N.-brokered 1994 peace accord.
Political observers in Luanda said immediate change was not likely, as political power stayed firmly in the hands of President Jose Eduardo dos Santos.
A Western diplomat said dos Santos and a handful of advisers ran the country from the secluded presidential palace, Futungo das Belas, on the outskirts of the capital.

"Policy decisions in Angola are meant to be made in the government through the council of ministers, the prime minister and so on. But in fact all the decisions are made by a very small group of people in Futungo," he told Reuters.
Another diplomat there would be little immediate change in the ministries occupied by UNITA -- geology and mines, tourism, trade and health.
New Geology and Mines Minister Marcos Samondo told Reuters he was already at his desk on Monday and had been warmly greeted by ministry staff.
He faces the tricky task of working with the state-run Endiama diamond company to transform the diamond areas in the northeast, controlled mainly by UNITA.
Samondo is expected to have some authority over diamond deals that could see the establishment of legal partnerships between UNITA and foreign companies.
UNITA's diamond wealth has generated an estimated $600 million annually, funding the war against the government and now the main source of party revenues.
But Samando says his priority is to diversify the country's approach towards exploiting Angola's resources.
"Right now my ministry has too much emphasis on diamonds," Samondo said.
"Angola is a mineral-rich nation, we need to take advantage of all our natural resources."
Analysts said parliament, which until now has sat with an MPLA majority and just some small opposition parties, will become the centre for real debate on policy issues and the country's future.
"Now there will be a very vocal opposition in the National Assembly for a change and the MPLA will be forced to answer some tough questions," said one analyst.
"With 70 members in the assembly, UNITA can deny MPLA the two-thirds majority they need to make constitutional change."
No parliamentary programme has yet been worked out, but one of the main focuses over the next two years will be rewriting the constitution, to be followed by elections.

"UNITA will definitely demand more transparency in the budgetary process, something that has so far not happened. UNITA will use this as ammunition during the next round of elections if the government is slow to deliver," the analyst said.

The MPLA of dos Santos went to war with UNITA shortly after independence in 1975. Millions of land mines still have to be cleared and a vast task of rebuilding devastated infrastructure awaits the new government.
